title: Getting Around
subtitle: Take the bus, buy a ticket and find your way in a French city

lessons.title: Les transports
lessons.description: Name the ways to travel around a city and use the verb "prendre" with each one.

blocks.heading: Taking the bus, the metro, the train
blocks.body: In French you "take" a means of transport, exactly like in English: "je prends le bus". The transport always keeps its article — le bus, le métro, le train — so never say « je prends bus ».

examples.french: Je prends le bus tous les matins.
examples.english: I take the bus every morning.

examples.french: Tu prends le métro ?
examples.english: Do you take the metro?

examples.french: Elle prend le train de huit heures.
examples.english: She takes the eight o'clock train.

examples.french: Nous prenons un taxi ce soir.
examples.english: We're taking a taxi tonight.

examples.french: Vous prenez la ligne 4.
examples.english: You take line 4.

examples.french: Ils prennent le tramway jusqu'au centre.
examples.english: They take the tram to the centre.

blocks.tip: Parisians say "le métro" for the underground and "le RER" for the fast suburban trains.

blocks.heading: Getting on and getting off
blocks.body: You get on with "monter dans" and get off with "descendre de". To ask where to get off, say "Je descends où ?" — the driver or another passenger will help you.

examples.french: Je monte dans le bus à la gare.
examples.english: I get on the bus at the station.

examples.french: Descendez à l'arrêt suivant.
examples.english: Get off at the next stop.

examples.french: Je descends où pour le musée ?
examples.english: Where do I get off for the museum?

examples.french: L'arrêt est devant la pharmacie.
examples.english: The stop is in front of the pharmacy.

examples.french: La station Bastille est fermée.
examples.english: Bastille station is closed.

examples.french: Le bus 27 passe toutes les dix minutes.
examples.english: Bus 27 comes every ten minutes.

blocks.tip: Buses and trams have "un arrêt" (a stop); the metro and trains have "une station" or "une gare".

blocks.heading: The verb prendre
blocks.body: "Prendre" is irregular but you will use it every day — for transport, food and drinks. Watch the plural forms: nous prenons has one n, ils prennent has two.

examples.french: Je prends le bus.
examples.english: I take the bus.

examples.french: Tu prends le métro ?
examples.english: Do you take the metro?

examples.french: Il prend le train à sept heures.
examples.english: He takes the train at seven.

examples.french: Nous prenons la ligne 1.
examples.english: We take line 1.

examples.french: Vous prenez un taxi ?
examples.english: Are you taking a taxi?

examples.french: Elles prennent le tramway.
examples.english: They take the tram.

blocks.tip: "Je prends" and "il prend" sound identical — the d and s at the end are both silent.

blocks.heading: en bus, à pied
blocks.body: To say how you travel, use "en" when you go inside the vehicle, and "à" when you sit on it or use your own legs. So: en bus, en voiture, en train — but à pied and à vélo.

examples.french: Je vais au travail en bus.
examples.english: I go to work by bus.

examples.french: Nous voyageons en train.
examples.english: We travel by train.

examples.french: Il part en voiture demain.
examples.english: He is leaving by car tomorrow.

examples.french: Elle va à l'école à pied.
examples.english: She walks to school.

examples.french: Je vais au parc à vélo.
examples.english: I cycle to the park.

examples.french: On arrive en avion samedi.
examples.english: We arrive by plane on Saturday.

blocks.tip: "À pied" never changes and never takes an article — it is always exactly these two words.

passages.title: Dans le bus
passages.french:
Julie habite loin du centre. Le matin, elle va à l'arrêt à pied.
Elle prend le bus 27, puis elle prend le métro, ligne 4.
— Excusez-moi, monsieur, je descends où pour le musée ?
— À la station Saint-Michel, madame. C'est le prochain arrêt.
— Merci beaucoup !
Le soir, son mari vient la chercher en voiture.
passages.english:
Julie lives far from the centre. In the morning, she walks to the stop.
She takes bus 27, then she takes the metro, line 4.
— Excuse me, sir, where do I get off for the museum?
— At Saint-Michel station, ma'am. It's the next stop.
— Thank you very much!
In the evening, her husband comes to pick her up by car.

lessons.title: Acheter un billet
lessons.description: Buy a train ticket, understand the departure time and find the right platform.

blocks.heading: At the ticket window
blocks.body: Start with "Bonjour", then "je voudrais" (I would like) — it is the polite way to ask for anything in France. The clerk will ask whether you want "un aller simple" (one way) or "un aller-retour" (return).

examples.french: Bonjour, je voudrais un billet pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: Hello, I would like a ticket to Lyon, please.

examples.french: Un aller simple ou un aller-retour ?
examples.english: One way or return?

examples.french: Un aller-retour, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: A return ticket, please.

examples.french: Deux places pour le train de midi.
examples.english: Two seats for the twelve o'clock train.

examples.french: Ça fait combien ?
examples.english: How much is it?

examples.french: Vous pouvez payer au distributeur.
examples.english: You can pay at the machine.

blocks.tip: Every station has "un distributeur" (a ticket machine) with an English option — but the queue at "le guichet" is often faster for complicated trips.

blocks.heading: Times and platforms
blocks.body: Timetables use the 24-hour clock: "le train de quatorze heures trente" is the 2.30 p.m. train. The platform is "le quai" and the track number is "la voie". Watch the boards for "départ" (departure) and "arrivée" (arrival).

examples.french: Le train part à quelle heure ?
examples.english: What time does the train leave?

examples.french: Il part à quatorze heures trente.

examples.english: The train is ten minutes late.

examples.french: L'arrivée à Marseille est à dix-huit heures.
examples.english: The arrival in Marseille is at 6 p.m.

blocks.tip: On regional trains you must validate your ticket before boarding: "N'oubliez pas de composter votre billet !"

blocks.heading: Je voudrais — asking politely
blocks.body: "Je veux" (I want) sounds blunt in French. "Je voudrais" (I would like) is the polite form and it is what everyone uses in shops and stations. It works with a noun or with another verb in the infinitive.

examples.french: Je voudrais un billet, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: I would like a ticket, please.

examples.french: Je voudrais deux places pour Lille.
examples.english: I would like two seats to Lille.

examples.french: Je voudrais partir demain matin.
examples.english: I would like to leave tomorrow morning.

examples.french: Je voudrais réserver une place.
examples.english: I would like to reserve a seat.

examples.french: Nous voudrions un aller-retour.
examples.english: We would like a return ticket.

examples.french: Vous voudriez payer par carte ?
examples.english: Would you like to pay by card?

blocks.tip: Add "s'il vous plaît" at the end and you will sound perfectly polite every single time.

blocks.heading: Asking with quel / quelle
blocks.body: "Quel" means "which" or "what" and must agree with the noun after it: quel quai (m), quelle voie (f), quels trains (m pl), quelles places (f pl). All four forms sound the same.

examples.french: À quelle heure part le train ?
examples.english: What time does the train leave?

examples.french: C'est quel quai ?

examples.french: Quelle voie, s'il vous plaît ?

examples.french: Quels sont les horaires du dimanche ?

examples.french: Quelles places avez-vous ?

examples.french: Le train de quelle heure ?
examples.english: The train at what time?

blocks.tip: In speech, French people often just say "C'est quel quai ?" with the question word at the end. It is correct and very common.

lessons.title: Trouver son chemin
lessons.description: Ask for directions in the street and understand the answer, with the imperative: tournez, continuez, traversez.

blocks.heading: Stopping someone and asking
blocks.body: Always begin with "Excusez-moi" or "Pardon" plus "madame" or "monsieur" — a French person will help much more willingly. Then ask with "Où est..." or "Je cherche...".

examples.french: Excusez-moi, madame, où est la gare ?
examples.english: Excuse me, ma'am, where is the station?

examples.french: Pardon, monsieur, je cherche la poste.
examples.english: Excuse me, sir, I'm looking for the post office.

examples.french: C'est loin d'ici ?
examples.english: Is it far from here?

examples.french: Je suis perdu, vous pouvez m'aider ?
examples.english: I'm lost, can you help me?

examples.french: Vous avez un plan de la ville ?
examples.english: Do you have a map of the town?

examples.french: C'est à combien de minutes à pied ?
examples.english: How many minutes is it on foot?

blocks.tip: A woman says « Je suis perdue » with an extra e. The pronunciation does not change.

blocks.heading: Understanding the answer
blocks.body: Answers use short instructions and a few landmarks: le feu (the traffic light), le carrefour (the crossroads), le pont (the bridge), le rond-point (the roundabout). Distances are usually given in minutes on foot.

examples.french: Non, ce n'est pas loin du tout.

blocks.tip: If you did not understand, just say « Pardon, vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ? » — nobody will mind.

blocks.heading: Giving instructions: the imperative
blocks.body: To tell someone what to do, take the "vous" form of the verb and drop the word "vous": vous tournez becomes tournez. This is the form used in every direction you will hear in the street.

examples.french: Tournez à droite au feu.
examples.english: Turn right at the traffic light.

examples.french: Continuez tout droit.
examples.english: Keep going straight ahead.

examples.french: Traversez le pont.
examples.english: Cross the bridge.

examples.french: Prenez la deuxième rue à gauche.

examples.french: Allez jusqu'au carrefour.

examples.french: Ne tournez pas ici.
examples.english: Don't turn here.
examples.note: negative: ne ... pas around the verb

blocks.tip: With a friend, use the "tu" form and drop the final s of -er verbs: tourne à droite, continue tout droit.

blocks.heading: Saying where things are
blocks.body: Place words end in "de", so they contract with the article: de + le = du, de + les = des. The same happens with "jusqu'à": jusqu'à + le = jusqu'au.

passages.title: Où est le musée ?
passages.french:
— Pardon, monsieur, je cherche le musée. C'est loin d'ici ?
— Non, c'est à cinq minutes à pied. Continuez tout droit jusqu'au feu.
— D'accord.
— Au feu, tournez à gauche et traversez le pont. Le musée est en face de la banque.
— Merci beaucoup, monsieur !
— Je vous en prie. Bonne visite !
passages.english:
— Excuse me, sir, I'm looking for the museum. Is it far from here?
— No, it's a five-minute walk. Keep going straight ahead as far as the traffic light.
— Okay.
— At the light, turn left and cross the bridge. The museum is opposite the bank.
— Thank you very much, sir!
— You're welcome. Enjoy your visit!
